Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I can't deal with even the slightest upset
The event happened because of the way I acted

vignette: As a firefighter, Alexandra had always prided herself on her ability to stay calm in high-pressure situations. But it was during a particularly harrowing call that everything changed. She and her team were responding to a hostage situation at a local bank, where several people were being held captive by an armed individual. As she entered the building, Alexandra was suddenly taken hostage herself, forced to spend hours in a cramped, dimly lit room with no clear escape route. The experience left her shaken, but it wasn't until weeks later that the full weight of what had happened began to sink in. Old photos from that day started surfacing online, and each time she saw one, Alexandra felt like she was transported back to that tiny room. The memories came flooding back – the smell of sweat, the sound of muffled screams, the feeling of helplessness. It was as if she was reliving it all over again, and yet, at the same time, the memory felt distant, like it belonged to someone else. As the days turned into weeks, Alexandra found herself becoming increasingly withdrawn. She started avoiding crowded spaces, unable to shake the feeling that she was being watched or trapped. The slightest noise would make her jump – a car backfiring, a door slamming shut – and she couldn't relax even when she knew she was safe. Her colleagues noticed the change in her, too, commenting on how "on edge" she seemed all the time. Alexandra couldn't shake the feeling that it was all her fault – if only she had acted differently, maybe things would have turned out okay. She started to doubt her own abilities as a firefighter, wondering if she was truly cut out for this line of work. Her identity, once so tied up in her bravery and composure, now felt fractured and uncertain. The memories of that day continued to haunt her, feeling more real than any other experience in her life. She could recall every detail with perfect clarity – the way the light filtered through the blinds, the sound of the perpetrator's voice, the feel of the handcuffs on her wrists. It was as if she had taken photographs of each moment, and they were forever seared into her mind. As the memories resurfaced, so did the negative thoughts. Alexandra felt like she couldn't deal with even the slightest upset – a minor disagreement with a colleague, a difficult call – without feeling completely overwhelmed. She began to wonder if she was truly capable of handling this job, or if she was just pretending to be something she's not. The cycle was vicious – the memories triggered by old photos or crowded spaces would lead to feelings of threat and anxiety, which in turn made her doubt herself even more. The negative appraisals fueled the memories, making them feel even more vivid and real. And so it went on, a self-reinforcing loop that seemed impossible to break. It was only when Alexandra found herself unable to respond to a routine call – frozen in fear as she approached the scene – that she realized she needed help. She couldn't keep living like this, constantly on edge, forever trapped in the memories of that terrible day. With a deep sense of trepidation, she made an appointment with a therapist, hoping against hope that somehow, someway, she could learn to escape the past and find herself again.
